text:
Recent work supports testing SASRec’s loss and negative coverage before adding architecture complexity. [gSASRec’s 2024 extended abstract](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/939) links sampled BCE to overconfidence and proposes generalized BCE; this is distinct from false-negative contamination. [eSASRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06450) identifies a strong combination of autoregressive training, LiGR layers, and sampled softmax, although its combined improvements do not isolate the loss effect. [Scalable-SASRec (RecSys 2024)](https://github.com/AIRI-Institute/Scalable-SASRec) supplies direct comparisons of multi-negative BCE, generalized BCE, sampled CE, and scalable CE. [LogQ correction research (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331) further cautions that the always-present positive requires different treatment from sampled negatives when deriving corrections.

Hard negatives warrant a curriculum and safeguards. [R²NS (WWW 2026)](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) reports that introducing hard negatives too early can underperform uniform sampling; its approach combines uniform warm-up, global candidate recall, and progressively harder stochastic selection. Sampling among top-ranked candidates reduces reliance on a single potentially false negative, but cannot establish irrelevance. A [2024 sampling comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) also finds dataset-dependent accuracy and popularity tradeoffs. Practical inference for this task: compare baseline BCE against sampled softmax with 16/64/256 negatives, then test a warm-start mixture of uniform and moderately hard negatives. Mask padding, target collisions, and known training positives; use only training histories for these controls. Select by pinned four-category macro validation HR@10 and inspect Electronics separately. Neither larger training margins nor these papers establishes an Electronics-specific gain.
